title: Electron-Induced Formation of C$_{2}$ on Si(100) from Acetylene and Ethylene
authors: Oliver MacLean, Marc Savoie, Damian G. Allis, Rafik Addou, Ryan Groome, Si Yue Guo, Aru Joy Hill, Alex Inayeh, Hadiya Ma, Cameron J. Mackie, Sheena Ou, Marco Taucer, Denis A. B. Therien, Finley Van Barr, Ryan Yamachika
abstract: Hydrogen Desorption Lithography on Si(100) demonstrates the ability of the Scanning Tunneling Microscope (STM) to create functional atomic-scale structures and devices. The dehydrogenation of adsorbed molecules represents a potential complementary technique that has received little attention. For example, formation of C$_{2}$ could introduce local strain or act as centers for subsequent reactions and would inform positionally controlled mechanosynthesis, an approach with vast potential in surface patterning and functionalization. Here, we studied the electron-induced dehydrogenation of acetylene and ethylene on Si(100) at 4 K using STM. Excitation of acetylene at +3.2 V and above induces configurational switching, including to a new sublayer-bonded geometry previously predicted to be an adsorption precursor, as well as migration and desorption. Excitation also induces dehydrogenation to C$_{2}$. Switching between three observed C$_{2}$ configurations can be induced by excitation at +4.2 V and above. Simulations using density functional theory reproduced the experimental images based on choice of functional, dimer-buckling averaging, and inclusion of diffuse basis functions. In addition, dehydrogenation could be induced using field-emitted electrons on a scale ranging from a single molecule to a radius of >10 nm. These observations highlight the potential of carbon dehydrogenation as an additional tool in Atomically Precise Fabrication (APF).
summary: This work uses STM and DFT to study how electrons trigger dehydrogenation reactions of adsorbed hydrocarbons ($	ext{C}_2	ext{H}_2$, $	ext{C}_2	ext{H}_4$) on $	ext{Si}(100)$. The key finding is that electron excitation causes the molecules to shed hydrogen atoms, forming stable carbon clusters ($	ext{C}_2$) in several distinct atomic arrangements. This demonstrates a powerful new tool for atomically precise surface functionalization.
main_problem: The study investigates electron-induced dehydrogenation of adsorbed hydrocarbons ($	ext{C}_2	ext{H}_2$ and $	ext{C}_2	ext{H}_4$) on the $	ext{Si}(100)$ surface to understand the formation of stable $	ext{C}_2$ species.
main_result: Electron excitation using STM induces configurational switching, migration, and dehydrogenation, leading to the formation of $	ext{C}_2$ in multiple distinct geometries ($	ext{IR-C}_2$, $	ext{OD-C}_2$, $	ext{ID-C}_2$).
method: The research combines Scanning Tunneling Microscopy (STM) experiments with Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations to model the electronic and structural changes.
model_or_system: The physical system is adsorbed acetylene or ethylene on a $	ext{Si}(100)$ surface, studied at cryogenic temperatures ($4 	ext{ K}$). The process involves electron tunneling excitation to drive chemical reactions.
key_observables: Configurational switching ($	ext{OD} \leftrightarrow 	ext{ID}$), dehydrogenation product formation ($	ext{C}_2$), and the observation of multiple stable $	ext{C}_2$ geometries.
important_parameters: Excitation biases (e.g., $\ge+3.2 	ext{ V}$, $\ge+4.2 	ext{ V}$), temperature ($4 	ext{ K}$), and applied current/voltage settings for STM.
main_assumptions: The interpretation relies on DFT simulations that must account for complex surface dynamics like dimer flipping, contrast inversion, and the stability of various adsorption intermediates.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate molecular displacements (switching, migration) induced by tunneling electrons; other figures show the new asymmetric feature ($	ext{UD}$) and evidence for $	ext{C}_2$ formation in different geometries.
paper_structure: The paper systematically presents STM observations of initial adsorption configurations, followed by characterization of structural changes upon electron excitation, culminating in the identification and simulation of dehydrogenation products.
why_interesting: While focused on surface chemistry, the use of controlled electronic excitation (STM bias) to drive chemical reactions is analogous to studying non-equilibrium quantum processes or localized energy deposition effects relevant to open quantum systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Tunneling-electron-induced molecular displacements of acetylene. All STM images are filled-state, and visualizations below show the position of the acetylene features on the Si lattice. (a,b) A switch from the OD (a) to ID (b) configuration induced by a +3.2 V pulse (average current >10 nA) over the center of the OD feature. (c,d) Long-range migration of OD-C2H2 induced by a +3.6 V pulse (4.6 nA). (e,f) Presumed desorption of OD-C2H2 induced by a +3.6 V pulse (2 nA). No new acetylene was observed within a radius of 6 nm. In each image, vertical lines indicate the center of the dimer rows and horizontal lines show the positions of three adjacent dimers. Imaging parameters: (a,b)...

Figure 2: Formation of a new acetylene configuration, interpreted as the under-dimer (UD) geometry, induced by tunneling-electron excitation. (a,b) Empty-state images showing conversion from ID-C2H2 to UD-C2H2 induced by a +3.4 V pulse (0.2 nA). Imaging parameters: (a,b) +2.0 V, 100 pA. See Figure S2 for a visualization of the UD-C2H2 geometry.

Figure 3: Formation of C2 by tunneling-electron excitation of acetylene. (a,b) Filled-state STM images showing dehydrogenation, along with a configuration change, of a UD-C2H2 to a new feature in an IR geometry induced by a +3.4 V pulse (4.5 nA). Imaging parameters: (a,b) −1.8 V, 50 pA.

Figure 4: Tunneling-electron-induced switching of C2. (a,b) Filled- and empty-state STM images showing the conversion of IR-C2 to OD-C2 by a +4.7 V pulse (>10 nA). The streakiness of the resulting OD- C2 feature is attributed to switching between two tilted orientations of the C2. Both polarities are included to make both the starting IR-C2 and ending OD-C2 features clear. (c,d) Filled-state STM images showing the conversion of IR-C2 to ID-C2 by a +4.7 V pulse (>10 nA). No empty-state image was recorded after the switching because the change is clear from filled-state imaging. Imaging parameters: (a) −2.0 V, 200 pA; +2.6 V, 100 pA (b) −2.4 V, 100 pA; +2.6 V, 100 pA (c) −2.0 V, 100 pA (d)...

Figure 5 shows the main acetylene and C2 features and the matching STM simulations. To reduce the possibility of excessive tailoring of the STM simulations to the experiment, the images in Figure 5 are presented with a single bias/energy and a common Z-scale for each polarity and experiment or simulation. A downward shift in magnitude was applied to the simulation energies relative to the experimental biases to account for experimental factors such as band bending32 and theoretical limitations including the absence of dopants and any issues related to the use of molecular proxies.
